html:
A domed Baroque church on the point between the Grand Canal and the Giudecca Canal in Venice, facing Piazza San Marco across the water. The plague that struck Venice in 1630 killed some 46,000 people in the city, nearly a third of them, and on 22 October 1630 the Senate vowed a church to the Virgin Mary as Our Lady of Health. A competition chose the design of Baldassare Longhena. Building began in 1631 and ended in 1681, the year before he died.

The church is an octagon under a great dome, with a second dome over the sanctuary and two bell towers behind, standing on a platform of about a million wooden piles. Longhena called it a crown for the Virgin. Chapels ring the central space. The high altar holds a Byzantine icon of the Virgin brought from Candia on Crete after the city fell to the Ottomans in 1669, under a marble group of the Queen of Heaven driving out the Plague. The sacristy holds paintings by Titian and Tintoretto's Marriage at Cana.

With Il Redentore, built after the plague of 1575 and 1576, it is one of Venice's plague churches. Each year on 21 November, the Festa della Madonna della Salute, Venetians cross the Grand Canal on a bridge of boats to give thanks here.
